title: Catherine the Dominican
hookLine: Catherine of Siena lived as a Dominican laywoman, at home, in a black cloak

lines: SHE WON'T MARRY. NO CONVENT, EITHER.
A WHITE DRESS, A BLACK CLOAK.
cards: Siena, in Italy. A dyer's house, loud with family, the smell of the vats drifting in from the work yard. One of the daughters won't marry.
Her family pushes; she refuses. She doesn't run off to a convent, either. She asks to join a group of local women who wear a white dress and a black cloak, and live in their own homes.

For a while she barely leaves a small room in her parents' house. Then she walks out of it, and doesn't stop: sickrooms, prisons, city councils, and eventually the pope's court. Her name was Catherine.
Today, the woman in the black cloak.

teach.h: THE MANTELLATE: A CLOAK, NOT A CLOISTER.
teach.b: You met Catherine of Siena back on day eighty-nine; today, the cloak she wore. The women were called the mantellate, from the Italian for a mantle, a cloak.
They belonged to the Dominican family as laywomen, doing penance and works of mercy, not as cloistered nuns. Catherine became a mantellata. She lived at home and went out into the city.

teach.h: THE SICK, THE PRISONERS, THE CONDEMNED.
teach.b: Her confessor, the Dominican Raymond of Capua, wrote her life, and tells of her nursing the sick and visiting prisoners.
In one of her own letters she describes sitting with a young man condemned to death, staying with him to the end. Matthew's Gospel names that kind of love.
In the Douay-Rheims: "I was sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." Then came the letters.

teach.h: LETTERS TO THE POPE IN AVIGNON.
teach.b: Catherine dictated letters to kings, city leaders, cardinals, and the pope himself, who was living in Avignon, in France, far from Rome.
She wrote to him plainly, with respect and with fire, urging him to come back to Rome and make peace.

teach.h: A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH, FROM HOME.
teach.b: Her thinking about God and the soul, gathered in a book called the Dialogue, is still read, and the Church calls her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone.

teach.h: I WAS SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.
teach.b: All from a laywoman in a cloak. Being a Dominican, she showed, isn't only for friars and nuns. It's a family with room at the kitchen table.

how: Lay Dominicans belong to fraternities attached to the Order of Preachers, making a promise, meeting to pray and study, and serving in ordinary life; Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a Doctor of the Church and read her Dialogue and letters.

games.q: you're a young woman in Siena. your family wants you married. you feel called to give your life to God, but not behind convent walls. what do you do?
o: join the mantellate and serve from home.
games.why: Catherine became a mantellata: a Dominican laywoman who lived at home, then walked out to the sick, the prisons and the pope.

practice: There are still lay Dominicans today, people with jobs and families who belong to the Dominican family and pray its prayers; bring them to mind.

Then widen the circle to someone you know who lives their faith without a habit or a title, the neighbor who drives people to chemo, the aunt who visits the nursing home; if you pray, ask Saint Catherine to pray for them, and if not, thank them silently, one by one.

wordCard.voice: Catherine the Dominican. Catherine of Siena, a mantellata: a Dominican laywoman in a black cloak who nursed, wrote and counseled popes from home. Today's word.

orig.note: Italian: a woman who wears the mantle, the black cloak of Siena's Dominican laywomen.

carryVoice: Your line: the mantellata. A cloak, not a cloister, and a whole city for a convent. Until tomorrow.
